name: Sumerian poems, Old Babylonian and Standard Babylonian versions of Gilgamesh (the layered textual tradition, including the Bilgames/Gilgameš name question)
date: Sumerian poems: known from Old Babylonian copies 'especially the eighteenth century bc, but they probably go back to a period of intense creativity under the patronage of King Shulgi of Ur (2094–2047 bc)' (A. R. George, 'The Epic of Gilgamesh', Cambridge Companion to the Epic, 2010, https://beckassets.blob.core.windows.net/product/readingsample/801345/9780521880947_excerpt_001.pdf). Old Babylonian Akkadian epic ('Surpassing all kings'): eighteenth century BCE manuscripts (same source). Middle Babylonian and peripheral versions, 1600-1000 BCE, from Babylonia, Hattusa, Emar, Ugarit and Megiddo (same source). Standard Babylonian epic ('He who saw the Deep'): standardised by Sîn-lēqi-unninni, who 'probably lived towards the end of the second millennium bc' (George, same source), 'sometime between 1300 and 1000 BCE' per https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Epic_of_Gilgamesh; oldest copies ninth or eighth century BCE, best copies from Ashurbanipal's Nineveh library (7th century BCE), last dated manuscript about 130 BCE (http://ancientworldonline.blogspot.com/2016/04/the-standard-babylonian-epic-of.html). Modern recovery: George Smith's 1872 reading of the Flood tablet; the Old Babylonian Pennsylvania tablet published by Stephen Langdon in 1917 (PBS X/3, https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/The_Epic_of_Gilgamish) and the Yale tablet by Jastrow and Clay in 1920 (https://www.gutenberg.org/files/11000/11000-h/11000-h.htm); Tigay's 'Evolution of the Gilgamesh Epic' 1982; Cavigneaux and Al-Rawi's Me-Turan edition of the Death of Gilgamesh 2000 (https://brill.com/display/title/7385?language=en); George's critical edition 2003 (https://bmcr.brynmawr.edu/2004/2004.04.21/); Rubio's name article 2012.
creator: Anonymous Sumerian court and school poets; Old Babylonian scribes and singers (George finds 'no sign of any one author who might have been responsible for the poem's original creation'); the Standard Babylonian text 'was associated in Babylonian tradition with the name Sîn-leqi-unninni, a scholar-exorcist who was claimed as an ancestor by scribes of Uruk' (George 2010, https://beckassets.blob.core.windows.net/product/readingsample/801345/9780521880947_excerpt_001.pdf). Modern reassembly by George Smith, Stephen Langdon, Morris Jastrow and Albert Clay, Samuel Noah Kramer, Jeffrey Tigay, Antoine Cavigneaux and Farouk Al-Rawi, Andrew George, Enrique Jiménez and the eBL team, with Gonzalo Rubio on the name question.
form: Physical clay tablets in cuneiform across several layers: five independent Sumerian narrative poems, an Old Babylonian Akkadian epic known only from scattered manuscripts of at least two versions, Middle Babylonian and western peripheral fragments, and a twelve-tablet Standard Babylonian Akkadian epic, reassembled by scholars into critical editions (George 2003; the eBL Corpus).
effect_on_arc: Each layer changes the story. The Sumerian poems 'are independent compositions and do not form a literary whole' (George 2010, https://beckassets.blob.core.windows.net/product/readingsample/801345/9780521880947_excerpt_001.pdf): Gilgamesh and Huwawa, Gilgamesh and the Bull of Heaven, Gilgamesh and Aga, Gilgamesh, Enkidu and the Netherworld, and the Death of Gilgamesh (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Epic_of_Gilgamesh). 'In the earlier Sumerian texts, Enkidu is Gilgamesh's servant' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gilgamesh); the Babylonian epic makes him a friend and equal, so his death drives the quest for immortality. In the Old Babylonian Sippar (Meissner) tablet the alewife tells Gilgamesh to accept death, enjoy life and start a family, which Bendt Alster called the first recorded carpe diem. In the Standard Babylonian Tablet X 'advice unrelated to the journey itself which she offers in the older version is absent'; she only explains the route and sends him to Urshanabi, and Andrew George treats the change as one of Sîn-lēqi-unninni's innovations (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siduri). The Standard Babylonian version also reframes the poem, opening 'He who saw the Deep' instead of 'Surpassing all kings' (George 2010), and closes on the view of Uruk from the wall. Tablet XII is 'a translation of the latter part of one of the Sumerian poems of Gilgamesh', related to the epic 'but not in form and structure' (George 2010); in it Enkidu goes down to the netherworld alive, after his death in Tablet VII. Names shift: in the Old Babylonian Sippar tablet the ferryman is Sursunabu, a name that 'no longer appears' in later versions (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Urshanabi), and the flood hero is 'here called Uta-na'ishtim' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Epic_of_Gilgamesh), later Uta-napishti. An even odder variant: the oldest Middle Babylonian fragment (MB Priv1, probably 16th century BCE) replaces Gilgamesh and Enkidu with the gods Sîn and Ea (George 2010).
critical_response: Tigay's 'The Evolution of the Gilgamesh Epic' (1982) set the model of an epic that grew by stages from Sumerian poems to the Standard Babylonian edition. George's two-volume 'The Babylonian Gilgamesh Epic' (Oxford, 2003) is the standard critical edition; BMCR called it a major advance on Campbell Thompson's 1930 edition (https://bmcr.brynmawr.edu/2004/2004.04.21/). George separates the sources into four periods and treats each as a distinct stage, 'showing that there is no single Epic of Gilgamesh: parts of different versions survive, spread across eighteen hundred years of history' (George 2010, https://beckassets.blob.core.windows.net/product/readingsample/801345/9780521880947_excerpt_001.pdf). His Penguin translation (1999) prints the Sumerian poems separately under the name Bilgames. On whether a Sumerian epic existed, George calls the Sumerian and Babylonian poems independent works sharing a likely oral inheritance, 'neither, however, is a translation of the other'; a Korean Journal of Old Testament Studies article argues 'it is reasonable to assume the existence of a Sumerian epic, at least in an oral form' (https://journal.kci.go.kr/ksots/archive/articleView?artiId=ART003124097) [uncertain: read from abstract only].
controversies: The Bilgames/Gilgameš name question. The Sumerian spelling has conventionally been read Bilgames (George's Penguin usage). Gonzalo Rubio, 'Reading Sumerian Names, II: Gilgameš', Journal of Cuneiform Studies 64 (2012): 3-16 (https://www.journals.uchicago.edu/doi/10.5615/jcunestud.64.0003), acknowledges this is 'a long-standing Assyriological convention' but concludes: 'there are good reasons to read Gilgameš, instead of "Bilgames," in Sumerian as well as in Akkadian' (quoted at https://languagelog.ldc.upenn.edu/nll/?p=73432). A related suggestion that the Sumerian name was Pabilgames 'is not supported by epigraphic or phonological evidence' (Wikipedia, as quoted in the same Language Log post). Other disputes: whether Sîn-lēqi-unninni composed or compiled; George notes that the later Uruk scribes' view that he advised a historical King Gilgamesh 'is anachronistic' (George 2010, https://beckassets.blob.core.windows.net/product/readingsample/801345/9780521880947_excerpt_001.pdf); whether Tablet XII belongs to the epic (it 'was probably appended at a later date', https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Epic_of_Gilgamesh); whether a unified Sumerian epic ever existed; and whether Gilgamesh was a historical Early Dynastic king of Uruk [uncertain: historicity not checked against a source here].
regional_reception: Every layer comes from what is now Iraq. George: the eleven Old Babylonian pieces are 'all from Babylonia itself'; Standard Babylonian copies come from Nineveh (Mosul), Asshur, Kalah/Nimrud, Babylon and Uruk (George 2010, https://beckassets.blob.core.windows.net/product/readingsample/801345/9780521880947_excerpt_001.pdf). Sumerian copies come mainly from Nippur and Ur, and Iraqi excavators at Me-Turan (Tell Haddad) recovered new Death of Gilgamesh fragments (https://brill.com/display/title/7385?language=en). Most Nineveh tablets went to the British Museum in the 19th century. In the Middle Babylonian period the poem was already international: 'parts of it have turned up at Megiddo in Palestine, Ugarit and Emar in Syria and Hattusa in Anatolia', with Hurrian and Hittite prose paraphrases (George 2010).
method: Classic cuneiform philology: identifying fragments in museum collections, physical joins of broken pieces, collating duplicate manuscripts line by line into a composite 'score' edition, and aligning parallel versions across periods. George 2003 separates the sources into four periods instead of interpolating early material into the late poem as Campbell Thompson did (George 2010, https://beckassets.blob.core.windows.net/product/readingsample/801345/9780521880947_excerpt_001.pdf). Since 2018 the eBL Fragmentarium at LMU Munich adds computational matching: a string-alignment algorithm run over human transliterations has 'found several matchings that had escaped human attention', including a new fragment of the latest datable Gilgamesh manuscript (https://iaassyriology.com/in-the-spotlight-the-electronic-babylonian-literature-project/).
ai_pipeline_stage: None for the historic reassembly of the Sumerian, Old Babylonian and Standard Babylonian layers, which was human philology. Recent additions to the Standard Babylonian text come partly from machine fragment matching (string alignment over transliterations) in the eBL Fragmentarium; imaging, reading and translation remain human (https://iaassyriology.com/in-the-spotlight-the-electronic-babylonian-literature-project/).
scale_metrics: George 2003: 'where Thompson's edition was based on 112 manuscripts, mine utilizes 218 pieces' (George 2010, https://beckassets.blob.core.windows.net/product/readingsample/801345/9780521880947_excerpt_001.pdf). Of these, 184 are first-millennium (Standard Babylonian era) fragments, counted at January 2003, against 108 for Campbell Thompson, 'some 25 of which are completely new to this edition' (https://bmcr.brynmawr.edu/2004/2004.04.21/; http://ancientworldonline.blogspot.com/2016/04/the-standard-babylonian-epic-of.html). The remainder match George's second-millennium counts: 11 Old Babylonian pieces giving 'a little over six hundred lines of poetry', from at least two versions, and 23 Middle Babylonian fragments (184 + 11 + 23 = 218). By about 2010 first-millennium sources had reached 'about 190', and 'since 2003 no fewer than ten pieces of the poem have become available' (George 2010). The Standard Babylonian poem 'is about two-thirds recovered; it must once have extended to about 3,600 lines' (George 2010; BMCR's reviewer gives 'some three thousand lines'). Five Sumerian poems. Since 2018 the eBL has added 20 Gilgamesh fragments touching more than 100 lines (NYT, 2024, per the eBL results file). Manuscripts span about 1,800 years.
what_was_found: Not a single find but a stack of them. The Nineveh Standard Babylonian tablets (Flood story on Tablet XI read by George Smith in 1872) gave the twelve-tablet frame. Old Babylonian tablets showed an earlier, differently shaped epic: the Pennsylvania tablet (Tablet II, bought 1914, said to come from Larsa; Enkidu's arrival in Uruk) and the Yale tablet (Tablet III, the Cedar Forest plans) (https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/The_Epic_of_Gilgamish; https://www.gutenberg.org/files/11000/11000-h/11000-h.htm); the Sippar (Meissner) tablet with the alewife's advice, Sursunabu and Uta-na'ishtim; and pieces from Tell Harmal, Ishchali and Nippur (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Epic_of_Gilgamesh). Sumerian school tablets from Nippur and Ur, plus the Me-Turan (Tell Haddad) finds for the Death of Gilgamesh (https://brill.com/display/title/7385?language=en), showed the episodic stories behind both, including the direct source of Tablet XII.
provenance_and_ethics: Nineveh tablets were excavated for the British Museum in the mid-19th century under Ottoman rule and remain in London. The Pennsylvania tablet was bought by the University Museum in 1914 through the market, with a findspot only 'said to' be Larsa (https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/The_Epic_of_Gilgamish). Me-Turan material came from Iraqi excavations (https://brill.com/display/title/7385?language=en). Looting remains live: the Gilgamesh Dream Tablet, looted from an Iraqi museum in 1991, bought by Hobby Lobby for almost $1.7 million in 2014, was forfeited in July 2021 and returned to Iraq in September 2021 (https://www.smithsonianmag.com/smart-news/hobby-lobby-forfeits-rare-gilgamesh-tablet-smuggled-iraq-180978314/). Some Old Babylonian manuscripts sit in private collections such as the Schøyen Collection (https://www.schoyencollection.com/literature-collection/babylonian-literature-collection/epic-gilgamesh-ms-3025) [uncertain: documented findspots of the Schøyen pieces not checked]. Digital copies are open through eBL (https://iaassyriology.com/in-the-spotlight-the-electronic-babylonian-literature-project/).
ai_craft_tension: The layered history shows that assembly has always been an editorial and literary act. Someone in the Old Babylonian period made a servant into a friend whose death breaks the hero; a later editor cut Siduri's advice about enjoying life (George's reading, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siduri), opened with 'He who saw the Deep', and the tradition kept Tablet XII even though it contradicts the plot. Machines now find matching fragments at scale (eBL string alignment), which extends the recovery work. They do not make the choices ancient editors made or that modern translators still make: which Siduri to print, whether to call the hero Bilgames or Gilgamesh, whether Tablet XII is an ending or an appendix. The name question is a good example. It turns on sign values, phonology and scribal convention, and Rubio's 2012 case is a scholar weighing evidence against 'a long-standing Assyriological convention'.
essay_hooks: 1) 'There is no single Epic of Gilgamesh: parts of different versions survive, spread across eighteen hundred years of history' (George 2010, https://beckassets.blob.core.windows.net/product/readingsample/801345/9780521880947_excerpt_001.pdf). 2) The numbers: Campbell Thompson had 112 manuscripts; George's 2003 edition used 218 pieces, 184 of them first-millennium; the Standard Babylonian poem is still only about two-thirds recovered (George 2010; https://bmcr.brynmawr.edu/2004/2004.04.21/). 3) In the Sumerian poems Enkidu is Gilgamesh's servant (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gilgamesh); the friendship that makes the epic work came later. 4) Siduri's 'enjoy life' advice, the part many readers remember, survives on one Old Babylonian tablet and is absent from the standard version (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siduri). 5) The oldest Middle Babylonian fragment swaps Gilgamesh and Enkidu for the gods Sîn and Ea (George 2010). 6) Tablet XII is a translation of half a Sumerian poem, attached so that dead Enkidu walks again. 7) Even the hero's name is contested: Bilgames by convention, but 'there are good reasons to read Gilgameš, instead of "Bilgames," in Sumerian as well as in Akkadian' (Rubio, JCS 64, 2012, quoted at https://languagelog.ldc.upenn.edu/nll/?p=73432). 8) People were still copying it about 130 BCE (http://ancientworldonline.blogspot.com/2016/04/the-standard-babylonian-epic-of.html).
